voice.speaker: Ryan
voice.instruct: Calm, clear and friendly, like a good teacher explaining an idea for the first time. Steady pace.

beats.s0b0: Every model in this story is three choices. A score function, a loss, and a way to minimize that loss.
beats.s0b1: And each new model exists because the one before it hit a wall. So for each one, watch for four things: the score, the loss, the wall, and the fix.
beats.s1b0: Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum. Y hat equals w times x, plus b. Its score function is a straight line.
beats.s1b1: The loss is squared error. Each vertical gap is a residual, and each square is that residual, squared.
beats.s1b2: Training picks the w and b that make the total area of those squares as small as possible. For linear regression there's a direct formula, so no iteration is needed.
beats.s1b3: Now let's use it for a yes or no label, coded as zero or one.
beats.s1b4: The line predicts values below zero and above one. Those can't be probabilities. And a straight line can't bend to fit anything curved. That's the wall.
beats.s2b0: Logistic regression keeps the weighted sum, z equals w x plus b, but reads it as log odds.
beats.s2b1: Then the sigmoid squashes any z into a probability between zero and one. The straight line becomes an S curve.
beats.s2b2: The loss is log loss. Each row pays minus the log of the probability it gave to its true class. Bigger rings mean bigger penalties.
beats.s2b3: Confident and right costs almost nothing. Confident and wrong costs a lot. Remember this loss, because XGBoost uses the same one.
beats.s2b4: Starting from a flat guess, gradient descent nudges w and b downhill on log loss, until the curve fits.
beats.s2b5: Here's the wall. The log odds have to be a straight line in x. So give it a class that lives in the middle of the range...
beats.s2b6: ...and the best S curve it can draw is nearly flat. It can't say high in the middle and low at both ends, unless you build that feature by hand.
beats.s3b0: A decision tree asks yes or no questions, like: is x less than three point six? Each leaf predicts the share of class one among its rows, so the score function is a step function.
beats.s3b1: The loss here is impurity. Gini impurity is zero for a pure leaf, and point five for a fifty fifty leaf.
beats.s3b2: Each split is chosen greedily. Try every possible cut, and keep the one that lowers the weighted Gini the most.
beats.s3b3: And it finds the bump in the middle, the one logistic regression couldn't, with no feature engineering at all.
beats.s3b4: The wall: let the tree grow deep, and it starts chasing every noisy label.
beats.s3b5: And if you retrain it on a slightly different sample of rows, you get a completely different tree. That's high variance. In other words, overfitting.
beats.s4b0: Random forest starts with bootstrap samples. Draw rows at random, with replacement. Some rows get drawn twice, and some never get drawn at all.
beats.s4b1: Grow a deep tree on each sample. The forest's score is just the average of every tree's prediction. That's the bold line.
beats.s4b2: There's no shared loss. Each tree minimizes Gini on its own sample, completely independently of the others.
beats.s4b3: Their random mistakes point in different directions, so they cancel out, and the variance drops.
beats.s4b4: The wall: no tree ever looks at what the others got wrong. So the mistakes they share survive the average. Those are circled.
beats.s4b5: To fix that, we need to build trees in sequence, each one aimed at whatever is still wrong.
beats.s5b0: In gradient boosting, the score is a sum of trees, in log odds. F of x is a base value, plus a small step from each tree. The base is the log prior odds, so the model starts flat, at the class share.
beats.s5b1: It uses the same log loss as logistic regression. Each row's gradient is p minus y. The arrows show how far each row wants its prediction to move.
beats.s5b2: Round one: fit a small tree to those gradients. Each leaf's value is minus G, over H plus lambda. The tree's output, scaled by the learning rate, gets added to F.
beats.s5b3: Then recompute the gradients and repeat. Rows that are already right stop pulling, and the rest keep pulling. Bias drops, one small tree at a time.
beats.s5b4: Forty shallow trees later, the curve fits the bump.
beats.s5b5: The wall: with deeper trees and more rounds, the training loss keeps falling, but the loss on held out rows turns back up. That's overfitting.
beats.s5b6: So XGBoost adds brakes. A learning rate, a maximum depth, lambda and gamma regularization, and early stopping at the best validation round.
beats.s6b0: Now, back to your problem. Say a region holds ten rare rows and nine hundred ninety majority rows, and the model gives the rare class a one percent chance there.
beats.s6b1: Each rare row pulls the rare score up, hard, with a gradient of minus point nine nine. Each majority row pushes it down just a little, with plus point zero one.
beats.s6b2: Add them up, and they cancel. Minus nine point nine, plus nine point nine, is zero. No tree splits here. The prior has won.
beats.s6b3: Now weight the rare rows by five, and the sum becomes minus thirty nine point six. The tree finally acts. A threshold shift does the same job, after training.
beats.s7b0: Here's the whole lineage on one screen. Each model's wall is exactly what the next one fixes.
